Content:
The circle above has center [MATH: C(1,1),] and the points [MATH: A(-1,3)] and [MATH: B(3,-1)] are endpoints of the diameter [MATH: \overline{AB}.]

Content:
The line [MATH: l] is the perpendicular bisector of the diameter [MATH: \overline{AB},] which means that

Content:
- [MATH: l] is perpendicular to [MATH: \overline{AB},] and
- [MATH: l] splits the line segment [MATH: \overline{AB}] exactly in half.

Content:
Since [MATH: l] bisects [MATH: \overline{AB},] it must pass through the circle's center.

Content:
Let's use this information to find the equation of [MATH: l.]

Content:
First, the slope of the diameter equals the slope of the segment [MATH: \overline{AB}.] So, the slope [MATH: m_1] of this segment is

Content:
[MATH: m_{1}|= (y_{2} − y_{1})/(x_{2} − x_{1}); = (− 1 − 3)/(3 − (− 1)); = (− 4)/(4); = − 1.]

Content:
Since [MATH: \overline{AB}] and [MATH: l] are perpendicular, the slope of the perpendicular bisector is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the diameter. So, the slope [MATH: m_2] of [MATH: l] is

Content:
[MATH: m_{2}|= − (1)/(m_{1}); = − (1)/((− 1)); = 1.]

Content:
Finally, since [MATH: l] passes through the center [MATH: C(1,1),] we can use the point-slope formula to get the equation of the perpendicular bisector:

Content:
[MATH: y − y_{1}|= m_{2}(x − x_{1}); y − 1|= 1 ⋅ (x − 1); y − 1|= x − 1; y|= x]

Content:
So, the perpendicular bisector [MATH: l] has the equation [MATH: y=x.]

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: m_1] and [MATH: m_2] be the slopes of the lines [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{JK}] and [MATH: l,] respectively.

First, we compute the slope of [MATH: \overset{\longleftrightarrow}{JK}] using the coordinates of points [MATH: J(-1,1)] and [MATH: K(3,3),] as follows:

[MATH: m_{1}|= (y_{2} − y_{1})/(x_{2} − x_{1}); = (3 − 1)/(3 − (− 1)); = (2)/(4); = (1)/(2)]

The slope of the perpendicular bisector is the negative reciprocal of the slope of the diameter. Therefore, the slope of [MATH: l] is

[MATH: m_{2}|= − (1)/(m_{1}); = − (1)/(((1)/(2))); = − 2.]

The line [MATH: l] passes through the point [MATH: P(1,2).] So, we can use the point-slope formula to write the equation of line [MATH: l] as

[MATH: y − y_{1}|= m_{2}(x − x_{1}); y − 2|= − 2(x − 1); y − 2|= − 2x + 2; y|= − 2x + 4.]
